Question: Consider a computer system in which processes can request and release one or more resources. Once a process has been granted a resource, the process has exclusive use of that resource until it is released. If a process requests a resource that is already in use, the process enters a queue for that resource, waiting until the resource is available. Which of the following will NOT deal effectively with the problem of deadlock?
Choices
A. Giving priorities to processes and ordering the wait queues by priority
B. Having a process request all its required resources when it first begins, and restarting if it cannot obtain them all
C. Numbering the resources and requiring that processes request resources in order of increasing number
D. Having processes time out and restart after a random interval of waiting
cot:
We need to decide which option will not deal effectively with the problem of deadlock. This is a classic deadlock prevention/avoidance question. Options:

A. Giving priorities to processes and ordering wait queues by priority – this can help avoid circular wait? Priorities can break hold-and-wait? Might be effective.

B. Having a process request all its required resources when it first begins, and restarting if it cannot obtain them all – this is the "all-or-nothing" approach, prevents hold and wait, effective.

C. Numbering the resources and requiring that processes request resources in order of increasing number – this imposes a linear ordering, prevents circular wait, effective.

D. Having processes time out and restart after a random interval of waiting – this is a recovery technique, not prevention. It may resolve deadlock eventually but not guarantee. It may not be effective in all cases. So likely D is the one that will NOT deal effectively.

Thus answer D.
